so.subjective:
* Patient is a 58-year-old female with a history of lung cancer, currently undergoing chemotherapy with cisplatin and etoposide.
* The patient reports no swelling in their legs.
* The patient reports that they are unaware of a family history of cancer or respiratory conditions.
* She reports worsening shortness of breath over the weekend, which is severe and interferes with her daily activities.
* She also reports pain when swallowing, which is constant and worsens in her chest area.
* She has experienced weight loss and fatigue, but no chest pain.
* She has been taking Zofran for nausea and has had some relief.
* She has not had an endoscopic evaluation of the esophagus or esophageal imaging studies such as a barium swallow.
* The patient expresses hope that lidocaine will help with the issue.

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: I'm 58 years old, and I'm female. I'm here because I've been having some shortness of breath and pain when I swallow, and I wanted to check in about how I'm doing with my treatment for lung cancer.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you please provide more details about the duration and severity of your shortness of breath and dysphagia, any associated symptoms such as chest pain, weight loss, or fatigue, and specifics about your lung cancer treatment, including the type, duration, and how well you have responded to it?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: The shortness of breath has been getting worse over the weekend, and it's pretty bad now—I can't even walk down the street without feeling out of breath. The swallowing pain started more recently, and it hurts every time I swallow, but food doesn't get stuck. I don't have chest pain, but I have been losing some weight and feeling more tired than usual. I'm on chemotherapy with a combination of drugs, and my last dose was a few days ago. I had some nausea and fatigue from it, but the medicine you gave me helped with the nausea.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you provide details about your past medical history, including any previous illnesses, surgeries, allergies, or family history of cancer or respiratory conditions?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: I don't have any significant past medical history other than the lung cancer diagnosis. I don't have any allergies, and I don't recall any surgeries. I don't know much about my family history, but I don't think there's a history of cancer or respiratory issues on my side.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you provide details about the specific chemotherapy regimen you are currently receiving, including the names of the drugs and their dosages?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: I'm on a combination of cisplatin and etoposide. I don't know the exact dosages, but I had my last dose a few days ago. I had some nausea and fatigue from it, but the Zofran you prescribed helped with the nausea.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you please provide your current vital signs, including your blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation? Additionally, could you describe any findings from your respiratory, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal examinations?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: My vitals are normal, and my pulse ox is okay. The doctor checked my neck and didn't find any swollen lymph nodes. My heart sounds were normal, and when he listened to my lungs, he heard some crackles, which he said might be from fluid. On my chest, he saw some redness, maybe from the radiation. I didn't have any swelling in my legs. He mentioned I have some inflammation in my lungs from the radiation, which is causing the shortness of breath and the pain when I swallow.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you provide the specific results of the chest imaging, including whether there is evidence of pleural effusion or radiation-induced lung injury?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: The chest X-ray showed mild radiation pneumonitis, which is inflammation of the lungs from the radiation treatment. The doctor mentioned there might be some fluid in my lungs, but he didn't specifically say there was a pleural effusion. I don't know the exact details of the imaging, but he said it's causing some of the shortness of breath and the pain when I swallow.

conversation_turns.speaker: Doctor
conversation_turns.text: Could you clarify whether the dysphagia has worsened since the start of radiation therapy, and whether the pain on swallowing is more pronounced at certain times or with certain foods?

conversation_turns.speaker: Patient
conversation_turns.text: The dysphagia has definitely gotten worse since starting the radiation therapy. The pain is constant every time I swallow, no matter what I eat or drink. It hurts more in my chest area, and it doesn't feel like it's getting better. It's been really hard to eat and drink because of it.
